completion.summary: You followed more than six million years of experiments that reshaped the skull, spine, pelvis, legs, and feet into varied forms of hominin bipedalism.
completion.title: Walking became a whole-body system

introduction: Bipedalism did not appear in one leap or along a straight ladder. Fossils preserve different combinations of climbing and walking traits, and several hominin forms overlapped. Each stop is evidence about a branching history, not necessarily a direct ancestor of the next.

steps.evidence: Comparative anatomy and motion studies show how an ape body can combine vertical climbing, suspension, terrestrial movement, and occasional bipedality.

image.alt: An adult chimpanzee walking on the forest floor
image.caption: Living chimpanzees combine climbing and terrestrial movement with occasional upright posture.

sources.label: Crompton et al., Journal of Anatomy (2008)

steps.summary: Chimpanzees climb, knuckle-walk, and sometimes stand or walk on two legs. Their flexible locomotion helps test hypotheses about the last shared ancestor, although chimpanzees themselves are not our ancestors.
steps.title: The starting point was versatile
steps.uncertainty: The last common ancestor may have differed substantially from every living ape, so chimpanzees provide constraints rather than a preserved starting form.

steps.evidence: The femur’s shape is most consistent with loading during upright walking, while two ulnae retain strong signals of arboreal behavior.

image.alt: Museum cast of the Sahelanthropus tchadensis cranium
image.caption: The Sahelanthropus cranium and fragmentary limb bones preserve debated evidence for early bipedality.

steps.summary: Sahelanthropus combines a skull carried in a potentially upright posture with limb bones interpreted as evidence for habitual bipedality alongside substantial tree climbing.
steps.title: Upright signals near seven million years
steps.uncertainty: Its placement near the human–chimpanzee split and the locomotor interpretation of incomplete bones remain actively debated.

steps.evidence: The partial skeleton known as Ardi preserves a shortened upper pelvis that could stabilize the trunk during walking and a foot still capable of grasping branches.

image.alt: Reconstructed bones of the Ardipithecus ramidus partial skeleton Ardi
image.caption: Ardi preserves a mosaic of traits associated with both upright walking and movement in trees.

steps.summary: Ardipithecus ramidus combined pelvic and femoral traits used in upright walking with a grasping big toe and anatomy suited to climbing. Early bipedality remained deeply arboreal.
steps.title: Walking without abandoning the trees
steps.uncertainty: Its exact gait, efficiency, and relationship to later hominins remain contested because the skeleton is incomplete and distorted.

steps.evidence: Footprint depth and shape capture heel contact and forward propulsion, while Lucy and other skeletons show how the hips and knees supported single-leg stance.

image.alt: Museum cast of the Lucy Australopithecus afarensis skeleton
image.caption: Lucy and the Laetoli footprints provide complementary evidence for habitual australopith bipedality.

steps.summary: The Laetoli trackways record hominins repeatedly walking on two feet. Australopithecus afarensis also had a short broad pelvis, inward-angled knees, and lower limbs adapted to habitual bipedality.
steps.title: Footprints record repeated strides
steps.uncertainty: The precise gait reconstructed from the prints is debated, and OpenTree lacks a positioned A. afarensis node, so the map uses a nearby fossil branch.

steps.evidence: Fragmentary limb bones and associated skeletons reveal locomotor diversity among early Homo and neighboring australopith lineages.

image.alt: Museum cast of a Homo habilis cranium against a dark background
image.caption: The fragmented Homo habilis record makes its locomotor anatomy difficult to reconstruct with confidence.

steps.summary: Fossils assigned to Homo habilis combine bipedal lower limbs with relatively long arms and other climbing-related proportions. The origin of Homo did not instantly produce a modern human body.
steps.title: A mosaic persists in early Homo
steps.uncertainty: Which postcranial fossils belong to H. habilis is disputed, making its body proportions and locomotion unusually uncertain.

steps.evidence: The Turkana Boy skeleton documents human-like limb proportions, while 1.5-million-year-old Ileret tracks record an arched foot and medial push-off.

image.alt: Reconstruction of the Turkana Boy Homo erectus skeleton
image.caption: The Turkana Boy skeleton shows the long-legged body proportions associated with terrestrial travel.
image.credit: Claire Houck from New York City, USA

steps.summary: Homo erectus had longer legs, shorter arms, and a body plan suited to sustained travel on the ground. Footprints preserve a pattern of foot motion broadly similar to ours.
steps.title: A long-legged terrestrial walker
steps.uncertainty: H. erectus varied across more than a million years and a vast range, so no single skeleton represents the entire lineage.

steps.evidence: Complete limb bones, joint surfaces, footprints, and pelvic anatomy show habitual upright walking adapted to a powerful Pleistocene body.

image.alt: Museum display of the La Ferrassie Neanderthal skeleton
image.caption: The La Ferrassie skeleton documents a robust but fully upright and habitual biped.

steps.summary: Neanderthals were fully committed bipeds with broad trunks, robust joints, and relatively short distal limbs. Their build altered locomotor costs without making their gait primitive.
steps.title: Different bodies, capable walkers
steps.uncertainty: Soft tissues and behavior do not fossilize directly, and biomechanical models disagree about the energetic consequences of Neanderthal proportions.

steps.evidence: Motion capture and force measurements show how extended hips and knees, pelvic rotation, elastic arches, and toe-off limit muscular work during walking.

image.alt: People walking upright along a city street in Nairobi
image.caption: Modern walking is a coordinated whole-body system rather than the product of a single anatomical change.

sources.label: Pontzer et al., Journal of Human Evolution (2009)

steps.summary: Modern human walking integrates an S-shaped spine, bowl-shaped pelvis, inward-angled knees, long legs, stiff arched feet, and aligned big toes into an economical stride.
steps.title: An efficient modern stride
steps.uncertainty: Human populations and individuals vary, and our gait is one recent outcome among many successful forms of hominin bipedalism.

subtitle: Follow the mosaic evolution of upright posture, stable hips, weight-bearing knees, arched feet, and an efficient human stride.
title: From Climbing Apes to Human Walking
